title: Projects
text: Our research focuses on understanding how biodiversity and ecosystem function respond to natural and anthropogenic disturbances, including fire, drought, and land use change. We use a combination of field studies, spatial analyses, and modeling approaches to address questions related to wildlife response to change, forest resilience, and biodiversity conservation in the face of global change. Our work is motivated by the need to inform management and policy decisions that promote sustainable ecosystems and biodiversity conservation.

Colorado Fires and Wildlife





A black bear on a trail camera




The 2020 wildfire season was record breaking across the world, with over 50,000 wildfires reported in the US alone. These fires are emblematic of changing fire regimes, with large severe fires becoming more frequent. Wildlife response to fire is often variable, highlighting the need to understand species response to changing fire regimes. We deploy Automated Acoustic Recording Units (ARUs) and camera traps to survey wildlife communities across three historic fires that burned in the Southern Rocky Mountains: the Cameron Peak, Mullen, and East Troublesome fires. Our work using camera traps to assess terrestrial mammal use of these burned areas is currently in review. Analyses using acoustic data to assess bird and bat responses are ongoing - stay tuned.

Forest management & western birds





A deer on a trail camera




Active forest management is practiced across US forests to achieve many objectives including reducing wildfire hazard, timber production, and wildlife habitat management. Understanding how these actions influence animal communities is important for successful multi-use management of public lands and wildlife conservation. To this end, we are conducting multiple projects investigating biodiversity response to forest treatments.
Adaptive Silviculture for Climate Change (ASCC)
As part of a long-term manipulative experiment we are testing how wildlife respond to three forest management strategies (i.e., resistance, resilience, and transition) across three distinct forest types in Colorado. We use acoustic recording units (ARUs) and remote cameras survey birds, bats, and terrestrial mammals within experimental units. To date, we have completed pre-treatment surveys and are beginning to test the immediate effects of different levels of tree removal. In the years to come we will examine long-term wildlife responses to changes in forest structure, composition, and succession.
Western birds’ response to forest treatments
In collaboration with researchers at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and Colorado State University, we investigated how 103 birds across the western United States responded to four common forest treatment types (prescribed fire, thinning, mastication, and clearcuts), as well as how responses vary by the extent of treatment across the landscape and time since treatment. Findings from this work are currently under review and we are excited to share implications for western forest and wildlife management soon.
Pinyon jay response to vegetation treatments
The pinyon jay is an important mutualistic species with pinyon pine species in the US southwest. The jay has also suffered a dramatic decades-long decline. This trend has spurred intensive interest in improving our understanding of pinyon jay ecology and in developing a conservation strategy to arrest population declines. To aid in this effort we used eBird participatory science data and broad-scale vegetation treatment data to assess how jays are affected by common treatment types (i.e., prescribed fire, thinning, and mastication), how these effects vary across seasons, time since treatment, and across baseline habitat conditions. This work is currently in review for publication.

title: People
text:
Current Researchers





Leah McTigue
Research Associate
Leah is an Ecological Research Associate with Colorado State University Warner College of Natural Resources, Forest and Rangeland Stewardship and the U.S Forest Service Rocky Mountain Research Station in Fort Collins. She received her master’s degree from the University of Arkansas in 2023 on wildlife response to urbanization in Northwest Arkansas. In her current role, she is assessing the impact of the 2020 wildfire season on wildlife in the Southern Rocky Mountains, specifically looking at the Cameron Peak fire, Mullen fire, and East Troublesome fire.
Email: leah.mctigue[at]colostate.edu  ·  Google Scholar  ·  CV







Hailey Boone
Postdoctoral Researcher
Hailey is a postdoctoral researcher with Colorado State University Warner College of Natural Resources, Forest and Rangeland Stewardship and with the U.S Forest Service Rocky Mountain Research Station in Fort Collins. She received her doctoral degree from Michigan State University in 2024, with a dissertation on Moose and wolf dynamics and their response to park recreation visitation in Isle Royale National Park. She received her master’s degree investigating predator-prey dynamics centered around white-tailed deer fawns from North Carolina State University in 2019. She is interested in wildlife response to anthropogenic-related disturbances, especially for large mammal species, but is currently warming up to birds.
Email: hailey.boone@colostate.edu  ·  Google Scholar  ·  CV

Lab Alumni





Merijn van den Bosch
Postdoctoral Researcher
Merijn’s worked as a postdoctoral research scientist at Colorado State University, in collaboration with the U.S Forest Service, studying the effects of climate-change induced drought on biodiversity. Currently, Merijn is a postdoctoral research scientist at Michigan State University, where he studies the ecology and management of Gray wolves in the Great Lakes region of the United States. Broadly, he is interested in Wildlife conservation and in assessing and mitigating the impacts of human activity on wildlife.

February 2026 - New article led by Leah McTigue, Merijn van den Bosch, and Hailey Boone was published in Global Change Biology, reviewing the global literature on drought effects on wildlife.
